svg.text: Eight modules, their public class, their key methods — and the direction dependencies are allowed to point
DEPENDENCY DIRECTION — everything flows one way: config → session → the things that do work → the CLI that wires them
Constructed once, passed down. Nothing mutates it, so no module can surprise another.
Takes config + account id, returns dicts. No AWS calls at all — so it is trivially testable.
THE pattern you noticed: a session captured as an object, handed to every collaborator by constructor.
Pure assembly. Given ids, returns the dict AWS wants. No calls, no state.
WORK — talks to AWS and to docker
Every ensure_* is safe to run twice. Every delete_* tolerates absence, so a half-built stack still
The other pattern you noticed: shell commands as typed methods, with the failure tail lifted into an
ORCHESTRATE — the only place ordering lives
Create-or-update in one verb: describe first, branch second. Idempotent from the caller's view.
Thin on purpose. It owns argument parsing and ordering — no AWS logic lives here.
Nothing constructs its own collaborators. Provisioner is handed an AwsSession; AwsSession is
handed a DeployConfig. So a test can pass a fake, and no module can reach out and surprise you.
Why the split is 8 files and not 1
Each file has exactly one reason to change: a name changes -> config; a permission changes ->
policies; the container shape changes -> taskdef. That is what 'single responsibility' buys you —
